title: What must be true of the angles between three radial arms?
description: A three-arm figure and a turned copy of it are drawn one on top of the other, and the three angles between the arms must land on each other. Because they land on each other they are equal, and they share the full turn. Keeko's doubt is that the three angles can be different, because only the arms have to match.
teaching_notes: One idea: angles that must land on each other are equal, and equal angles round a point share three hundred sixty degrees. Watch for students who think only the arms need to match.

source: If a figure with three radial arms has rotational symmetry,
video_script.why: The child reasons that the three angles of a rotationally symmetric three-arm figure are equal and finds their size.

video_script.anchor: the book's three-arm figure and its turned copy, drawn one beside the other
video_script.wrong_answer: the three angles can be different
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says only the arms have to match, so the angles can differ.
video_script.payoff_line: The three angles are equal, one hundred twenty degrees each

final_answer.value: The three angles are equal: 360 ÷ 3 = 120° each
final_answer.spoken: the three angles are equal, three hundred sixty divided by three is one hundred twenty degrees each

hold_back: The three angles are equal: 360 ÷ 3 = 120° each
maths_rules: if the figure has rotational symmetry, a turned copy overlaps the original
the first angle overlaps the second, the second overlaps the third, the third overlaps the first
angles that overlap are equal, so the three angles are equal
the three angles share the full turn: 360 ÷ 3 = 120
